It is answered: This is a matter in which feet have slipped and disputation has been prolonged, and we will mention some of what has reached us from the words of the imams of Islam.

Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said in his book *Gharib al-Hadith* (The Strange Words of Hadith), which, along with the books of *gharib* that followed it, is an imam's work: "I asked Muhammad ibn al-Hasan about the interpretation of this hadith, and he said: 'This was at the beginning of Islam, before the obligations were revealed, and before the Muslims were commanded to fight (*jihad*).'"

Abu Ubayd said: "As for Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, he was asked about the interpretation of this other hadith: 'The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the children of polytheists, and he said: "God knows best what they were doing."'"

Abu Ubayd said: "He went to the view that they are born upon what they will become, whether disbelief or Islam."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "Abu Ubayd related these two views and did not commit himself to either an opinion or a preference in this matter."

Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi said in his book *al-Radd ala Ibn Qutaybah* (The Refutation of Ibn Qutaybah): "It is said to him: What is wrong with a man who relates a disagreement about a matter, and the correct position has not become clear to him, so he refrains from advancing what he has not clearly understood? There is no fault in this. Rather he is praiseworthy for abstaining from what has not become clear to him, perhaps it will become clear to him. The blameworthy defect is the one who ventures to speak about what he has no knowledge of, interpreting the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ) in a way that contradicts the ruling of the Book, departs from the sayings of the people of knowledge, and abandons analogy and reasoning, saying something that is unfit for a report and does not stand on sound reasoning.

This critic of Abu Ubayd claims that the *fitrah* upon which every child is born, as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed, is that in every child God creates knowledge (*ma'rifah*) of his Lord, and he claims that this is according to the meaning of God's saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify against themselves: "Am I not your Lord?"﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172], and so on.

Muhammad ibn Nasr said: God said: ﴿And God brought you out of the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾ [al-Nahl 16:78]. So this one claims they know the greatest of things, namely God, Exalted is He. Who is greater in sin and more opposed to the Book than the one who hears God, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿And God brought you out of the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾, and yet claims that they know the greatest of things? This is one who opposes the Lord of the worlds and is ignorant of the Book."

I say: If Abu Muhammad (Ibn Qutaybah) meant by "knowledge" the second knowledge that is actual (*bil-fi'l*), which belongs to adults, then Abu Abd Allah's (Ahmad's) rejection of it is directed correctly. But if he meant that the child is prepared for knowledge, and that knowledge is in him potentially, just as he is prepared for action and speech, then what Abu Abd Allah stated does not necessarily follow.

As if it were said: he is born speaking and rational, such that when he reaches the age of reason he recognizes his Lord through that faculty which Allah deposited in him, unlike inanimate things. Thus, if he were left to what he was created upon, and his natural disposition (fitra) were not altered, he would know his Lord, affirm His oneness, and love Him.

If it is said: Abu Abdullah (Ahmad ibn Hanbal) did not deny this. He only denied that the fitra means the first covenant which Allah, glorified is He, took from the children of Adam from their loins when He made them testify against themselves: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and they affirmed it. There is no doubt that this knowledge and affirmation are not present in the child, so Abu Abdullah's denial is valid.

It is said: Ibn Qutaybah only said that the fitra is that He created in every newborn a knowledge of his Lord, in the sense of His words: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and so on. This does not necessitate that this knowledge is actually present in the newborn. His comparing the hadith to the verse in this meaning does not indicate that the covenant mentioned in the verse is actual knowledge before they came out into this world alive and speaking. Although this has been said by more than one of the early generations (al-Salaf) and later generations (al-Khalaf), it does not follow that Ibn Qutaybah must choose this view. Rather, this is from the goodness of his understanding of the Qur'an and the Sunnah, as he took the hadith in light of the verse and explained each of them by the other. Many scholars before him and after him have said this. The best explanation of the verse is his, ﷺ, saying: "Every child is born upon the fitra; then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian."

So the covenant which He took from them, the testimony He made them bear against themselves, and the affirmation they made is the fitra upon which they were created, because He, glorified is He, argued against them with it. He does not argue against them with something none of them knows or remembers, but rather with something they all share in knowing and affirming.

Also, He said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; He did not say "from Adam," then He said "from their loins" and did not say "from his loin," then He said "their descendants" and did not say "his descendants," then He said: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This requires their affirmation of His lordship, an affirmation by which the proof is established against them. This is indeed the affirmation with which He argued against them through His messengers, like His saying: ﴿Their messengers said: Is there doubt about Allah?﴾ [Ibrahim: 10], and His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 87], ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25], and ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know? They will say, "To Allah"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 84-85]. Similar examples are many: He argues against them with what they were created upon of affirming their Lord and Originator, and calls them through this affirmation to worship Him alone and not to associate anything with Him. This is the method of the Qur'an.

Among this is the verse in al-A'raf, which is His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], to the end of the verse. For this reason He said at its end: ﴿Lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"; or lest you say, "It was only our fathers who associated partners with Allah before, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172-173]. He argued against them with what they affirmed of His lordship, to prove the invalidity of their polytheism and their worship of others, and to prevent them from making excuses, either by heedlessness of the truth or by blind imitation in falsehood. Misguidance has two causes: either heedlessness of the truth, or the imitation of the people of misguidance. Thus the hadith agrees with the verse, and each clarifies the meaning of the other. Ibn Qutaybah did not oppose the Lord of the worlds, nor did he ignore the Book, nor did he depart from reason. But when Abu Abdullah thought that the meaning of the verse is that Allah, glorified is He, brought them out alive and speaking from the loins of Adam all at once, then addressed them, spoke to them, took the covenant from them, made them testify against themselves of His lordship, then returned them into his back, and that Abu Muhammad (Ibn Qutaybah) explained the fitra with this very meaning, he held him to what he held him to.

Then Muhammad ibn Nasr said: Ibn Qutaybah argued with His saying: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Fatir of the heavens﴾ [Fatir: 1], meaning Creator of them, and with the words of the believer of Pharaoh's family in Surah Ya-Sin: ﴿And why should I not worship He who created me (fatarani)﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22], meaning "khalaqani," and with His saying: ﴿The fitra of Allah upon which He created people; there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. He said: Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, used to recite this verse when narrating this hadith, to show that the fitra is creation (khilqa).

Muhammad ibn Nasr said: It is said to him: We do not oppose you that the fitra in language is creation, and that Fatir of the heavens and earth is their Creator. But what is the evidence that this creation is knowledge? Do you have any proof from the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger that creation is knowledge? If you bring proof from the Book of Allah or the Sunnah of His Messenger that creation is knowledge, then well and good; otherwise you are a falsifier in your claim, and you are saying what you have no knowledge of.

I say: Neither Ibn Qutaybah nor anyone who said his statement, "the fitra is creation," meant that it is knowledge actually present in the newborn at the moment of birth. No one has said this. Ahmad, in the narration of al-Maymuni, said: "The first fitra is that upon which people were created." Al-Maymuni said to him: "Is the fitra the religion?" He said: "Yes."

He also stated in more than one place that if a disbelieving person's parents, or one of them, die, the child is judged to be Muslim, and he cited the hadith: "Every child is born upon the fitra," interpreting the hadith as meaning he is born upon the fitra of Islam, as is stated explicitly in another hadith. If that were not his meaning, his citing of it would not be valid, especially with a wording in some narrations: "No child is born except upon this millah (religion)."

As for Ahmad's statement in other places: "He is born upon what he was created upon, of wretchedness or happiness," there is no contradiction between this and his saying that it is the religion. Allah, glorified is He, decreed wretchedness and happiness and recorded them, and they occur through causes, such as the actions of the parents: their making him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. All this occurs by what Allah, exalted is He, has decreed. The child is born upon the fitra as a Muslim, and is born with this pure fitra which his parents may alter, as Allah decreed and recorded. This is as the Prophet ﷺ illustrated when he said: "Just as an animal gives birth to a complete young, do you see any mutilation in it?"

He thus clarified that the animal is born whole, then people mutilate it, and that too is by the decree and destiny of Allah. Likewise the child is born upon the fitra as a Muslim, then his parents corrupt him. Ahmad and others only said "he was born upon what he was created upon, of wretchedness or happiness" because the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) used to argue with this hadith that disbelief and sins are not by the decree of Allah, but by what people do; since every child is born upon the fitra, and his disbelief after that is from people. For this reason, when Malik was told: "The Qadariyya argue against us with the beginning of the hadith," he said: "Argue against them with its end," which is his saying: "Allah knows best what they were doing." The imams clarified that there is no proof in it for the Qadariyya. He did not say that the parents created his Judaism and Christianity, and the Qadariyya do not say that; rather they hold that he became a Jew or a Christian by his own choice, but the parents were a cause in this occurring through teaching and instilling. This is a truth which does not require negating the predestination that precedes from knowledge, the Book, and the will. Rather, that is attributed to Allah, exalted is He, as knowledge, writing, and will; to the parents as a means, teaching and instilling; to Satan as adornment and whispering; and to the servant as consent, choice, and love.

This is not contradicted by his saying in the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the boy whom al-Khidr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever, and had he lived he would have burdened his parents with rebellion and disbelief.

Its meaning is that it was decreed and predetermined in Umm al-Kitab (the Preserved Tablet) that he would be a disbeliever. This is a "predetermined state" (hal muqaddara), like His saying: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Nahl: 29], and His saying: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet﴾ [al-Saffat: 112], and similar examples. The intended meaning is not that his disbelief was actually existing along with him until he was sealed, as one says: "He was born a king," "he was born a scholar," "he was born a tyrant." Whoever thinks that the "sealing" mentioned in the hadith is the "sealing" in His saying: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾ [al-Nahl: 108] has clearly erred, for that is not said of it: "sealed on the day he was sealed," since sealing upon the heart occurs only after disbelief.

[Section: The evidence that the intended meaning of fitra is religion]

What confirms the correctness of what the imams explained the fitra as, namely that it is "the religion," is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i, from the Prophet ﷺ, relating from his Lord, blessed and exalted is He: "Indeed I created My servants as hunafa' (upright monotheists), all of them, but the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion, and forbade them what I had made lawful for them, and commanded them to associate with Me what I had not sent down any authority for."

This is explicit that they were created upon the hanifiyya (pure monotheism), and that the devils cut them off from it after that and drew them out of it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut (false deities); they bring them out from the light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. This includes the devils' taking them out from the light of the fitra into the darkness of disbelief and polytheism, and from the light which the messengers brought of guidance and knowledge into the darkness of ignorance and misguidance.

In the Musnad and others, from the hadith of al-Aswad ibn Sari', he said:

"The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent a military expedition, and the killing reached the offspring. The Prophet ﷺ said to them: 'What made you kill the offspring?'

They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, were they not the children of polytheists?' He said: 'Are not the best of you the children of polytheists?' Then the Prophet ﷺ stood up to give a sermon and said: 'Indeed every child is born upon the fitra until his tongue speaks for him.'" His sermon to them with this hadith, following his prohibition of killing the children of polytheists, and his saying to them: "Are not the best of you the children of polytheists?", explicitly states that he meant they were born non-disbelievers, and disbelief occurred afterward. Had he meant that the newborn at birth is either a disbeliever or a Muslim according to what the decree had preceded, what he mentioned would not have been an argument for what he intended by his prohibition to them against killing the children of polytheists.

Some have thought that the meaning of his saying: "Are not the best of you the children of polytheists?" is: perhaps it had preceded in Allah's knowledge that if they lived they would believe; so the prohibition would refer to this sense of possibility. But this is not the meaning of the hadith. Rather, its meaning is: your best are the foremost early Emigrants and Helpers, and these are children of polytheists, for their fathers were disbelievers, then the sons embraced Islam afterward. A child is not harmed by being a child of polytheists if he is a believer, for Allah rewards him by his own deeds, not by the deeds of his parents. He, glorified is He, brings forth the living from the dead, brings forth the dead from the living, the believer from the disbeliever, and the disbeliever from the believer.

This hadith, the hadith of the fitra, has wordings which explain one another. In the two Sahihs, with the wording of al-Bukhari, from Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 30, verse 30 (part 3 of 3):

"The Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition). Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you notice any mutilation in it?» Then Abu Hurayrah said: Recite: ﴿The nature (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no change in the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. They said: O Messenger of Allah, what about one who dies young? He said: «Allah knows best what they used to do.»"

In the Sahih it is related that al-Zuhri said: "Prayer is offered over every child who dies, even if he was born of illegitimacy, because he was born upon the fitrah of Islam, provided he cried out upon emerging. Prayer is not offered over one who did not cry out, because he was a miscarriage." And that Abu Hurayrah used to narrate that the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"«Every child is born upon the fitrah, and then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you notice any mutilation in it?»" Then Abu Hurayrah said: ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30].

In the Sahih, in the narration of al-A'mash: "«Every child is born upon the millah (religious community)»." In the narration of Abu Mu'awiyah from him: "«Upon this millah, until his tongue expresses it»." This is explicit that he is born upon the millah of Islam, as Ibn Shihab, the narrator of the hadith, explained it, and Abu Hurayrah's citing of the verse indicates this.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Ibn Shihab was asked about a man who owed a believing slave to free: Is it sufficient for him to free an infant who is still nursing? He said: Yes, because he was born upon the fitrah.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said, after mentioning the views of people on this hadith:

Others said: The fitrah here is Islam. They said: This is well known among the majority of the early generations (salaf), and the exegetes have agreed on the interpretation of the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30], to the effect that they said: the fitrah of Allah is the religion of Islam.

They argued by the words of Abu Hurayrah in this hadith: "«Recite, if you wish: ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]»."

He said: They also mentioned from Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, al-Dahhak and Qatadah, regarding the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30], that they said: the fitrah of Allah is the religion of Islam. ﴿There is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30]: they said: to the religion of Allah.

They argued by the hadith of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Thawr ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn Jabir, from Abd al-Rahman ibn A'idh al-Azdi, from Iyad ibn Himar al-Mujashi'i, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people one day: "«Shall I not inform you of what Allah has told me in the Book? Verily Allah created Adam and his children as hunafa' (upright) Muslims, and gave them wealth that is lawful, with nothing unlawful in it, but they made what Allah had given them unlawful and lawful»." The hadith continues.

He said: Likewise Bakr ibn Muhajir related from Thawr ibn Yazid, with his chain, the same in this hadith: "«hunafa' Muslimin»."

Abu Umar said: This hadith is related from Qatadah, from Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah, from Iyad ibn Himar, but Qatadah did not hear it from Mutarrif; rather he said: "Three told me: Uqbah ibn Abd al-Ghafir, Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir, and al-Ala' ibn Ziyad, all of whom said: Mutarrif told me, from Iyad, from the Prophet (ﷺ)," and in it he said: "«Verily I created My servants as hunafa', all of them»," without saying "Muslimin."

Likewise al-Hasan related it from Mutarrif, from Iyad.

Ibn Ishaq related it from one not accused, from Qatadah, with his chain, and he said in it: "«Verily I created My servants as hunafa', all of them»," and did not say "Muslimin."

He said: This indicates the retentiveness, precision and accuracy of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, for he mentioned "Muslimin" in his narration from Thawr ibn Yazid of this hadith, and omitted it from the narration of Qatadah. Thus people related it from Qatadah falling short of the word "Muslimin," while Thawr added it with his chain. Allah knows best.

Abu Umar said: In Arabic usage, hanif means the upright, the sincere, and there is no uprightness greater than Islam. He said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "The hanifiyyah is the pilgrimage to the House." This indicates that he meant Islam. Likewise it is related from al-Dahhak and al-Suddi: "hunafa': pilgrims," and from Mujahid: "hunafa' following." He said: All of this indicates that hanifiyyah is Islam.

He said: Most scholars said: the hanif is the sincere one. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The religion of your father Abraham; He named you Muslims before this﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. al-Ra'i said:

"O caliph of the Most Merciful, we are a people / hunafa', prostrating morning and evening"
"An Arab people in whose wealth we see Allah / the due of zakah sent down as a sending down"

He said: Thus he described hanifiyyah with Islam, and this is a clear matter with no concealment. He said: Among what those who held that the fitrah in this hadith is "Islam" argued by is his saying ﷺ: "«Five are of the fitrah»," and it is related: "«Ten are of the fitrah»," meaning the fitrah of Islam. End.

Our shaykh said: The proofs indicating that he meant the fitrah of Islam are numerous, such as the words of the authentic hadith cited earlier, like his saying: "«upon the millah»" and "«upon this millah»," and his saying: "«I created My servants hunafa'»," and in the other narration: "«hunafa' Muslimin»," and like the interpretation of Abu Hurayrah, and he knows best what he heard.

Had the intended meaning of fitrah not been Islam, they would not have asked after this: "«Do you see one of the children of the polytheists who dies while young?»" For if there were nothing that changes that fitrah, they would not have asked, and prior knowledge and the preceding Decree do not change.

His saying: "«Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian»" clearly indicates that they change the fitrah upon which he was created by this.

Also, he likened this to the animal born with complete form and no defect, which is then mutilated afterward. So it is known that change applies to the sound fitrah upon which the servant was born.

Also, the hadith corresponds to the words of the Most High: ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30], and this encompasses all people. Thus it is known that Allah created all people upon His aforementioned fitrah. The fitrah of Allah He attributed to Himself as an attribution of praise, not of blame, so it is known that it is a praiseworthy fitrah, not a blameworthy one. This is shown by His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, upright, the fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. This is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) implied by the first verb, according to Sibawayh and his companions. Thus it indicates that setting one's face toward the religion as a hanif is the fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind, as in its parallels, such as His saying: ﴿The Book of Allah upon you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], and His saying: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed before, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 62]. According to them this is a verbal noun in the accusative governed by a necessarily implied verb indicated by the preceding verb, as if he said: "Allah prescribed that for you." Likewise here: Allah created mankind upon that, upon establishing the religion as hanif.

The predecessors also explained it thus. Ibn Jarir said regarding this verse: He says: So direct your face toward the direction which Allah directed you, O Muhammad, to obey Him, which is the religion as hanif, meaning "upright in His religion and obedience." ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]: he says: "the workmanship of Allah upon which He created mankind." The accusative of fitrah is as a verbal noun from the sense of His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion as hanif﴾ [al-Rum: 30], for the meaning of the verse is: Allah created mankind upon that as a fitrah.

He said: The exegetes said things similar to what we have said. Then he related from Ibn Zayd, who said: "The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind: it is Islam, since Allah created them all from Adam, they acknowledge this," and he recited: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed we were unaware of this"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This is the saying of Allah: ﴿Mankind was one community, then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], [afterwards].

Then he mentioned with an authentic chain from Mujahid, who said regarding ﴿The fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]: "The religion is Islam."

Ibn Humayd related to us: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us: Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq related to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Maryam, who said: Umar passed by Mu'adh ibn Jabal and said: "What sustains this community?" Mu'adh said: "Three, and they are the saviours: sincerity, which is the fitrah ﴿the fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]; prayer, which is the millah; and obedience, which is the protection." Umar said: "You have spoken truly."

Then he said: Ya'qub al-Dawraqi related to me: Ibn Ulayyah related to us: Ayyub related to us, from Abu Qilabah, that Umar said to Mu'adh: "What sustains this community?" and he mentioned something similar.

He said: As for His saying: ﴿There is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], it means: there is no alteration of the religion of Allah, that is, that is not right and should not be done.

Abd Allah ibn Idris related from Layth, who said: Mujahid sent a man called Qasim to Ikrimah to ask him about ﴿There is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], and he said: "to the religion of Allah."

Then he mentioned from Ikrimah regarding ﴿the fitrah of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30]: "It is Islam."

Likewise it is related from Qatadah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about castrating animals, and he disliked it and said: ﴿There is no change in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30].

Likewise said Ikrimah, and Mujahid in the narration of Layth from him.

Our shaykh said: There is no contradiction between the two statements from them, just as the Most High said regarding Satan: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will cut off the ears of cattle; and I will surely command them, and they will alter the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 119]. Altering what Allah created His servants upon in religion is an alteration of His religion, and castration and cutting off the ear are an alteration of His creation. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) likened one to the other in his saying: "«Every child is born upon the fitrah, and then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you notice any mutilation in it?»" Those alter the religion, and these alter the form by mutilation and castration: this alters what Allah created the heart upon, and that alters what He created the body upon.

[Section: The Station of Repentance Turning Back (al-Inabah)]
[The Meaning of Inabah and Evidence for It]

You have known that whoever descends from the station of repentance (tawbah) and stands in its place has descended into all the stations of Islam, for complete repentance encompasses them, and they are included within it. Yet it is necessary to single out each one for mention and detailed explanation, to clarify its realities, its distinctive features, and its conditions.

When one's foot is firmly established in the station of repentance, he then descends to the station of inabah (turning back to God in devotion). God Most High has commanded it in His Book and praised His intimate friend (khalil) for it, saying: ﴿And turn penitently to your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 54], and He said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, plaintive, and penitent (munib)﴾ [Hud: 75].

He also informed that only the people of inabah are able to perceive and be reminded by His signs, saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We constructed it and adorned it?﴾ [Qaf: 6], until He said: ﴿An insight and a reminder for every servant who turns penitently (munib)﴾ [Qaf: 8]. He Most High also said: ﴿It is He who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky, and none remembers except one who turns penitently (yunib)﴾ [Ghafir: 13]. And He Most High said: ﴿Turning penitently to Him, and fear Him, and establish the prayer﴾, the verse.

Here "munibina" (turning penitently) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun implied in His saying "﴿So set your face﴾." Because this address is to him and to his community; that is, set your face, you and your community, turning penitently to Him. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. It is also permissible that it be a state of the object in His saying ﴿the nature upon which He created mankind﴾, meaning He created them turning penitently to Him. For if they were left alone and their natural disposition (fitrah), they would not have turned away from turning penitently to Him, but they change and deviate from that upon which they were created, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Every child is born upon the fitrah,» and in another narration: «upon the religion (millah), until his tongue expresses it.»

He also said concerning His prophet David: ﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord, and fell down bowing and turned penitently (anab)﴾ [Sad: 24].

He also informed that His reward and Paradise are for the people of fear and inabah, saying: ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the righteous, not far away. This is what you were promised, for every returner who keeps [his covenant], who feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a penitent heart (qalb munib). Enter it in peace﴾ [Qaf: 31–34].

He, glorified be He, also informed that good tidings from Him are only for the people of inabah, saying: ﴿And those who avoid the taghut, not worshipping it, and turn penitently to Allah, for them are good tidings﴾ [al-Zumar: 17].

Inabah is of two kinds: inabah to His lordship (rububiyyah), which is the turning of all created beings, shared by believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked. God Most High said: ﴿And when harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning penitently to Him﴾ [al-Rum: 33]. This is general with respect to every supplicant who is afflicted by harm, as is the reality. This kind of inabah does not necessitate Islam; rather, it coexists with polytheism and disbelief, as God Most High said concerning these people: ﴿Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a faction of them associates others with their Lord, so as to deny what We have given them﴾ [al-Rum: 33]. This is their condition after their inabah.

The second kind of inabah is the inabah of His friends (awliya'), which is inabah to His divinity (ilahiyyah), the inabah of servitude (ubudiyyah) and love (mahabbah).

It comprises four matters: loving Him, submitting to Him, turning toward Him, and turning away from all else. No one deserves the name munib except one in whom these four are gathered, and the explanation of the early generation (salaf) for this term revolves around this.

The word carries the meanings of hastening, returning, and advancing. The one who turns penitently to God (munib ila Allah) is the one who hastens to His pleasure, returns to Him at every time, and advances toward what He loves.

The author of al-Manazil said: "Inabah linguistically means returning, and here it means returning to the Truth." It consists of three things: returning to the Truth in amendment, as one returns to Him in apology; returning to Him in fulfillment, as one returns to Him in covenant; and returning to Him in state, as one returns to Him in response.

Since the penitent has returned to God through apology and abandoning His disobedience, it is part of completing that that he returns to Him through striving and sincere counsel in obedience, as He said: ﴿except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], and He said: ﴿except for those who repent and make amends﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160]. Repentance with idleness does not benefit; there must be repentance and righteous action: abandoning what He dislikes, doing what He loves, withdrawing from His disobedience, and adorning oneself with His obedience.

Likewise, returning to Him through fulfilling His covenant, as you returned to Him when the covenant was taken from you, for you returned to Him by entering under His covenant first; so upon you is returning by fulfilling what you pledged to Him second. The whole religion is a covenant and fulfillment, for God took His covenant from all the accountable to obey Him: He took His covenant from His prophets and messengers through the tongue of His angels, or from Him directly to the messenger without intermediary, as He spoke to Moses; He took His covenant from the nations through the messengers; and He took His covenant from the ignorant through the scholars. So He took the covenant from these through teaching and from those through learning. He praised those who fulfill His covenant and informed of the great reward they have with Him, saying: ﴿And who fulfills what he covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

He said: ﴿And fulfill the covenant, for the covenant will be questioned﴾ [al-Isra: 34], and He said: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you pledge﴾ [al-Nahl: 91], and He said: ﴿And those who fulfill their covenant when they make one﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

This includes their covenants with God, by fulfilling to Him with sincerity, faith, and obedience, and their covenants with creation.

The Prophet (ﷺ) informed: «Among the signs of hypocrisy is treachery after a covenant.»

So whoever betrays His covenant and deceives regarding it has not turned penitently to God, just as one who has not entered under His covenant has not turned to Him. Inabah is not realized except by commitment to the covenant and fulfillment of it.

His saying: "and returning to Him in state, as you returned to Him in response": that is, He, glorified be He, has called you, and you answered Him with "Here I am (labbayka) and at Your service (sa'dayka)" in word. So there must be a response in state that confirms the speech, for states confirm or contradict words, and every statement is witnessed for its truth or falsehood by the state of its speaker. So just as you returned to God in response with speech, return to Him in response with your state.

Al-Hasan said: "Son of Adam! You have speech and action, and your action is more deserving of you than your speech. You have an inner self and an outward self, and your inner self is more within your control than your outward self."

[Section: Returning to God]

He said: "Returning to Him in amendment is only upright through three things: exiting from obligations (tabi'at), grieving over stumbles, and making up for missed things."

Exiting from obligations is by repentance from sins between the servant and God, and paying the rights that are owed to creation. Grieving over stumbles has two possibilities:

The first: that one grieves over his own stumble when he stumbles, so his heart is pained and cracks. This is evidence of his turning to God, unlike one whose heart feels no pain and does not crack from his stumble, for that is evidence of the corruption and death of his heart.

The second: that one grieves over the stumble of his believing brother when he stumbles, to the extent that it is as if he himself stumbled, and does not gloat over him. This is evidence of the softness of his heart and his inabah.

Making up for missed things is making up for what he missed of obedience and devotion with their equivalents, or with something better than them, especially in the remainder of his life, as his departure to God approaches. The remainder of a believer's life has no price; he makes up with it what has passed, and revives with it what he has killed.

(Section)

He said: "Returning to Him in covenant is only upright through three things: freedom from the pleasure of sin, abandoning contempt for the heedless out of fear for them, along with hope for yourself, through thoroughly seeing the cause of service (the defects in one's service)."

When inabah is pure for him toward his Lord, he is freed from the thought of the pleasure of sin, and in its place he finds pain and grief for remembering it and thinking about it. As long as the pleasure of thinking about it still exists in his heart, his inabah is not pure.

If it is said: Which of the two states is higher: the state of one who finds the pleasure of sin in his heart, so he struggles against it for God and abandons it out of fear, love, and reverence for Him; or the state of one whose pleasure in sin has died in his heart, and in its place is pain, grief, tranquility toward his Lord, calm in Him, delight in His love, and sweetness in His remembrance?

It is said: The state of the latter is more complete and higher. The utmost goal of the one who struggles is to strive against his soul until he reaches the station and rank of this one, yet he follows him in rank and nearness and is connected to him.

If it is said: Then where is the reward of the struggle of the one who has the pleasure, and his abandoning what he loves for God, and his preferring God's pleasure over his desire? For this reason the human kind was preferred over the angelic kind according to the People of the Sunnah, and they were the best of creation. The tranquil one has rested from the pain of this struggle and been spared from it, so there is as much difference between them as between the rank of the healthy and the afflicted.

It is said: The soul has three states: commanding evil, then blaming oneself for it and regretting it, then tranquility to its Lord and turning fully toward Him. This last state is the highest of its states and most exalted, and it is what the struggler aspires to. What he gains of reward for his struggle and patience is for his striving toward the rank of tranquility in God. So he is like one who travels through deserts, wastelands, and terrors to reach the House, so his heart may be at rest by seeing it and circling it. The other is like one who is occupied with Him, circumambulating, standing, bowing, and prostrating, with no turning to anything else. The former is occupied with the means, the latter with the end. Each has a reward, but between the reward of ends and the reward of means there is a wide gulf.

What the tranquil one attains of states, worship, and faith surpasses what this struggler for the sake of God attains, even if the latter performs more deeds. The measure of the deeds of the tranquil, penitent one as a whole and in their manner is greater, even if this struggler has more deeds. That is God's grace, which He gives to whom He wills. Al-Siddiq did not surpass the Companions through abundance of deeds, though there were among them those who fasted, performed Hajj, recited, and prayed more than he did; rather, it was through another matter that stood in his heart, to the point that the most excellent of the Companions would race him and never see him except ahead.

Yet the servitude of the one who struggles against his soul over the pleasure of sin and desire may be harder, but its hardship does not necessitate its preference in rank. The best deed is faith in God, and jihad is harder than it and comes after it in rank. The rank of the siddiqin is higher than the rank of the mujahidin and the martyrs. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (radiya Allahu anhu), the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned the martyrs and said: «Most of the martyrs of my nation are the people of the beds, and many a slain man between the two rows—Allah knows best his intention.»

[Section: Signs of Inabah]

Among the signs of inabah is abandoning contempt for the heedless and fear for them, along with your opening the door of hope for yourself: you hope for mercy for yourself, and fear punishment for the heedless. Rather, hope for them mercy, and fear for yourself punishment. If you must nonetheless look down on them and hate them because of the exposure of their conditions to you and seeing what they are upon, then be more hateful toward yourself than toward them, and be more hopeful for them of God's mercy than you are for yourself.

Some of the early generation said: "You will not truly understand (tafqah) until you hate people for God's sake, then return to yourself and hate it even more."

This statement is not understood in its meaning except by a jurist (faqih) in the religion of God, for whoever witnesses the reality of creation, their weakness, their frailty, their shortcoming, indeed their negligence, their neglect of God's right, their turning toward other than Him, and their selling their portion from God for the cheapest price of this fleeting world, will find no alternative but to hate them, and it is absolutely impossible for him to do otherwise. But when he returns to his own self, his condition, and his shortcoming, and is aware of that, he will hate and despise himself even more. This is the jurist.

As for thoroughly seeing the causes of service (ilal al-khidmah), it is searching for what mixes with it of the desires of the soul, and distinguishing God's right within it from the soul's share. Perhaps most of it, or all of it, is a share for your soul while you are unaware.

So there is no god but Allah. How many obstacles, ulterior motives, and desires lie within the soul that prevent deeds from being purely for Allah and from reaching Him? A servant may perform a deed where no human sees him at all, yet it is not sincerely for Allah. And he may perform a deed while eyes surround him on every side, yet it is sincere for the Face of Allah. Only people of insight and physicians of the hearts, who know their diseases and their ailments, can distinguish between these.

Between the deed and the heart there is a distance, and in that distance are highwaymen who prevent the deed from reaching the heart. So a man may do much work, yet nothing from it reaches his heart: no love, no fear, no hope, no asceticism regarding this world, no desire for the Hereafter, and no light by which he distinguishes between the friends of Allah and His enemies, and between truth and falsehood, nor any strength in his affair. Had the effect of the deeds reached his heart, it would have been illuminated and would have shone. He would have seen truth and falsehood, distinguished between the friends of Allah and His enemies, and that would have brought him further states.

Then between the heart and the Lord there is also a distance, and upon it are highwaymen that prevent the deed from reaching Him: pride, self-admiration, presumption, seeing one's deed (as one's own), forgetting the favor (of Allah), and hidden ailments which, if one searched thoroughly for them, one would find wondrous things. It is among the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, that He conceals them from most workers. For if they saw them and witnessed them, they would fall into what is even worse: despair, hopelessness, belittling (of their deeds), abandoning works, dullness of resolve, and weakness of aspiration. For this reason, when the "Ri'aya" (Observance) of Abu 'Abdullah al-Harith ibn Asad al-Muhasibi appeared and the worshippers occupied themselves with it, mosques that they used to fill with worship were left deserted. The skilled physician knows how to treat souls: he does not build a palace while demolishing a city.

(Section)

He said: Returning to Him in the present state is only correct through three things: by despairing of your deeds, by witnessing your need, and by the flash of the lightning of His gentleness toward you.

Despair of one's deeds is explained by two things:

The first: that when one looks with the eye of reality at the True Agent and the First Mover, and realizes that were it not for His will, no act would come from you, then His will is what made your act happen, not your will. If He willed it, it would not remain without action. Here the contemplation of divine decree benefits, and so does annihilation from seeing one's deeds.

The second: that you despair of being saved by your deed, and you see that salvation is only by His mercy, His grace, and His favor, as in the Sahih (authentic collection) from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "No one among you will be saved by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and favor." So the first meaning relates to the beginning of the act, and the second to its end and outcome.

As for witnessing one's need: when one despairs of his deed at the beginning, and despairs of being saved by it at the end, he witnesses in every atom of himself a complete necessity for Him. His necessity is not from this aspect alone, but from all aspects. The aspects of his necessity cannot be counted, nor do they have a single cause. Rather, he is in need of Him in His essence, just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is self-sufficient in His essence. For self-sufficiency is an essential attribute of the Lord, while poverty, need, and necessity are an essential attribute of the servant.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his soul, said:

"Poverty is for me an inseparable essential attribute, always,
just as self-sufficiency is always an essential attribute of Him."

As for the flash of the lightning of His gentleness toward you: when one realizes a necessary power (of need), and despairs of his deed and of being saved by it, he looks at the gentleness of Allah and sees its flash. He knows that everything he is in, everything he hopes for, and everything that has preceded for him is a gentleness from Allah toward him, a favor He bestowed upon him, and a charity He gave him without any cause from him. For He is the Doer of good through the means and through what the means produce, and the command belongs to Him before and after. He is the First and the Last; there is no god but Him, and there is no lord besides Him.

[Section: Sins Cause Corruption on the Earth]

Among the effects of sins and disobedience is that they cause various kinds of corruption on the earth, in the waters, the air, the crops, the fruits, and the dwellings. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return.﴾ [al-Rum: 41].

Mujahid said: "When a wrongdoer takes charge, he spreads injustice and corruption, so Allah withholds the rain because of that, and the crops and the offspring are destroyed. Allah does not love corruption." Then he recited: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return.﴾ [al-Rum: 41].

Then he said: "By Allah, it is not your sea that is meant here, but every town situated on flowing water is a sea."

Ikrimah said: "Corruption has appeared on land and sea." He added: "Indeed I do not say to you, 'your sea,' but every town on water."

Qatadah said: "As for the land, it refers to the people of the open country (al-'Amud), and as for the sea, it refers to the people of towns and villages (al-Rif)." I say: Allah the Exalted has also called sweet water a sea, when He said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, palatable, pleasant to drink, and that one is salty and bitter.﴾ [Fatir: 12].

There is no sea in the world that is sweet and still; rather, there are only flowing rivers, and the salt sea is the still one. So the towns upon which flowing waters lie are named after those waters.

Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾: "It means the sins."

I say: He meant that sins are the cause of the corruption that appeared. If he meant that the corruption which appeared is the sins themselves, then the lam in His saying ﴿so that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ would be the lam of consequence and not of purpose. According to the first view, what is meant by corruption is loss, evil, and the afflictions that Allah brings upon the earth when the servants disobey. Whenever they commit a sin, Allah brings about a punishment for them, as one of the early generations (al-Salaf) said:

"Whenever you commit a sin, Allah brings about for you a punishment from His dominion."

The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the corruption intended refers to sins and what they necessitate. This is confirmed by His saying ﴿so that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾. This is our situation: He has only made us taste a small part of our deeds. Had He made us taste all of our deeds, He would not have left upon its surface a single creature.

Among the effects of disobedience to Allah on the earth is what befalls it of sinking and earthquakes, and what destroys its blessing. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by the dwellings of Thamud and forbade them from entering their dwellings except while weeping, and from drinking their waters, and from drawing water from their wells, until he commanded that the dough kneaded with their water not be fed to the camels, because of the ill effect of the evil of sin upon the water.

Likewise is the evil effect of sins on the lessening of fruits and the afflictions that you see.

Imam Ahmad mentioned in his Musnad, within a hadith, that he said: "Wheat was found in the treasuries of some of the Banu Umayyah, each grain the size of a date stone, and it was in a bag on which was written: 'This used to grow in a time of justice.'" Many of these afflictions were brought about by Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, because of the sins the servants have committed.

A group of the elders of the desert told me that they used to see the fruits larger than they are now, and that many of these afflictions which strike them, they did not know them, but they came about recently.

The effect of sins on forms.

As for the effect of sins on forms and creation, al-Tirmidhi narrated in his Jami' from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah created Adam, and his height in the heaven was sixty cubits, and creation has continued to diminish until now."

When Allah wishes to purify the earth from the oppressors, the treacherous, and the wicked, He brings forth a servant from His servants, from the family of His Prophet (ﷺ), who will fill the earth with justice as it has been filled with injustice. The Messiah will kill the Jews and the Christians, and he will establish the religion with which Allah sent His Messenger, and the earth will bring forth its blessings and return as it was, so much so that a band of people will eat a pomegranate and shelter under its shell, a cluster of grapes will be the load of a camel, and the milk of one she-camel will suffice a large group of people. This is because when the earth became pure of sins, the traces of blessing from Allah appeared in it, which sins and disbelief had destroyed. There is no doubt that the punishments which Allah sent upon the earth have left their traces flowing in the earth, seeking what resembles them of sins, which are the traces of those crimes for which the nations were punished. So these traces in the earth are among the traces of those punishments, just as these sins are among the traces of those crimes. Thus the word of Allah and His universal decree agree, at the beginning and at the end, and the greatest punishment corresponds to the greatest offense, and the lesser to the lesser.

Thus He, the Glorified, judges between His creatures in the abode of the barzakh (the intermediate realm) and in the abode of recompense.

Consider the companionship of Satan, his place, and his abode. When he accompanies a servant and gains control over him, the blessing is removed from his life, his deeds, his speech, and his provision. And when his obedience has an effect on the earth, the blessing is removed from every place where his obedience appears. Likewise, his dwelling, since it is Hellfire, contains nothing of spirit, mercy, or blessing.

(Section)

Know that Allah, the Glorified, perfected everything He made, and beautified everything He created. At the beginning of its creation, it is free from afflictions and defects, complete in the benefit for which it was prepared and created. Afflictions only befall it afterwards, through other causes such as proximity or mixing and blending, or other causes that necessitate its corruption. Had it been left in its original creation without the causes of corruption attaching to it, it would not have been corrupted.

Whoever has knowledge of the conditions of the world and its origin knows that all corruption in its atmosphere, its plants, its animals, and the conditions of its inhabitants is newly arising after its creation, through causes that required its occurrence. The deeds of the children of Adam and their opposition to the Messengers have not ceased to bring upon them general and particular corruption that draws upon them pains, diseases, sicknesses, plagues, drought and barrenness, and the removal of the blessings of the earth, its fruits, and its plants, and the removal or diminution of its benefits, as successive matters, one following another. If your knowledge cannot encompass this, then suffice yourself with His saying: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned.﴾

Apply this verse to the conditions of the world, and match what actually happens with it. You see how afflictions and defects arise at all times in fruits, crops, and animals, and how from those afflictions further afflictions arise that accompany them, some seizing the necks of others. Whenever people commit injustice and immorality, their Lord, Blessed and Exalted, brings upon them afflictions and defects in their food and fruits, their air and their water, their bodies and their creation, their forms, their shapes, and their characters, of deficiency and affliction, which is the necessary consequence of their deeds, their injustice, and their immorality.

Grains such as wheat and others used to be larger than they are today, just as the blessing in them used to be greater.

Imam Ahmad narrated with his chain that he found in the treasuries of some of the Banu Umayyah a bag containing wheat like date stones, on which was written: "This used to grow in the days of justice." This story he mentioned in his Musnad after a hadith he narrated.

Most of these general diseases and afflictions are a remnant of a punishment with which past nations were punished. Then a remnant of them remained, reserved for those who still retain a remnant of their deeds, as a just judgment and a fair decree. The Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to this with his saying about plague: "It is a remnant of a scourge or a punishment that was sent upon the Children of Israel."

Likewise, Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, unleashed the wind upon a people for seven nights and eight days, then He left in the world a remnant of it in those days, and in its likeness there is admonition and lesson.

Allah, the Glorified, has made the deeds of the righteous and the wicked necessitate their effects in this world, a necessity that cannot be avoided. He made the withholding of kindness, zakat, and charity a cause for the withholding of rain from the sky, and for drought and barrenness. He made the oppression of the needy, the defrauding in measures and weights, and the strong transgressing against the weak a cause for the tyranny of kings and rulers who show no mercy when asked for mercy, and do not show compassion when asked for compassion. In reality, they are the deeds of the subjects appearing in the forms of their rulers. Allah, the Glorified, in His wisdom and justice, shows people their deeds in molds and forms suited to them: sometimes through drought and barrenness, sometimes through an enemy, sometimes through unjust rulers, sometimes through general diseases, sometimes through worries, pains, and griefs which their own souls bring upon them and from which they never separate, sometimes through the withholding of the blessings of the sky and the earth from them, and sometimes through the empowering of devils over them, urging them urgently toward the causes of punishment, so that the word may be fulfilled against them, and so that each of them may arrive at what he was created for. The intelligent person travels with his insight through the regions of the world and observes it, and sees the places of Allah's justice and wisdom. Then it becomes clear to him that the Messengers and their followers in particular are upon the path of salvation, and the rest of creation are travelling upon the path of destruction, and heading toward the abode of ruin. Allah accomplishes His command; there is no repeller of His judgment and no averter of His order. And success is from Allah.

(Exhortation)

The earth has shuddered, the sky has darkened, and corruption has appeared on land and sea from the injustice of the wicked. Blessings have departed, goodness has become scarce, wild animals have become emaciated, and life has been embittered by the immorality of the oppressors. The light of day has wept, and the darkness of night has wept, because of the evil deeds and the monstrous actions. The noble recording angels and the successive angels have complained to their Lord about the abundance of abominations and the prevalence of evils and vices.

By Allah, this is a warning of a torrent of punishment whose clouds have gathered, and an announcement of a night of calamity whose darkness has become thick. So withdraw from the path of this way through sincere repentance while repentance is still possible and its door is still open. You are as if you were at the door when it has been closed, and at the pledge when it has been forfeited, and at the wing when it has been hung up. ﴿And those who did wrong will soon know what a [terrible] return they will have.﴾

(Chapter)

The winds of mercy are also called "the bringers of glad tidings" (al-mubashshirat), "the spreaders" (al-nashr), "those that scatter" (al-dhariyat), "those sent forth" (al-mursalat), "the gentle breeze" (al-rakhaa'), and "the fertilizing winds" (al-lawaqih). The winds of punishment are called "the violent" (al-'asif) and "the crushing" (al-qasif), both of which are at sea; and "the barren" (al-'aqim) and "the howling" (al-sarsar), both of which are on land. If He wills, He moves it with the movement of punishment, so He makes it barren and deposits in it a painful punishment, and makes it a retribution upon whomever He wills among His servants; so He makes it a howling wind, and a calamitous one, and a raging one, and one that corrupts whatever passes over it. The winds differ in their characteristics, and in their benefit and effect there is the greatest variety. There is a soft, moist wind that nourishes plants and the bodies of animals; another that dries them; another that destroys and ruins them; another that strengthens and hardens them; and another that weakens and enfeebles them.

For this reason, He (glorified is He) speaks of the winds of mercy in the plural form, because of the variety of their benefits and of what results from them: there is a wind that stirs up the clouds, a wind that fertilizes them, a wind that carries them on its backs, and a wind that nourishes plants. Since the winds differ in their characteristics and natures, He made for every wind a counter-wind that breaks its force and blunts its sharpness, while its gentleness and mercy remain. So the winds of mercy are many. As for the wind of punishment, it is a single wind, sent from a single direction to destroy what it is sent to destroy, so no other wind stands against it to oppose it or break its force or repel its sharpness. Rather, it is like a mighty army that nothing can resist, destroying everything upon which it passes. Reflect upon the wisdom, the sublimity and the eloquence of the Qur'an, how it applied this on land. As for the sea, the wind of mercy there came in the singular form, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice in it, there comes upon them a violent wind and the waves come at them from everywhere﴾.

Indeed, ships only move by one wind which comes from one direction. When the winds conflict over ships and oppose one another, their course is not completed. So the purpose of them at sea is the opposite of their purpose on land, since at sea the purpose is that it be one, good, and opposed by nothing. Thus it is singular here and plural on land. Furthermore, He (glorified is He) gave this subtle creature, which is moved by the weakest of creatures and which tears through things, such strength, force and might that it disturbs solid, strong, resistant bodies, dislodges them from their places, crushes them and carries them on its back. Look at it, despite its subtlety and lightness: when it enters a waterskin, for example, and fills it, then a heavy body such as a man or other is placed upon it and leans on it to submerge it in water, it cannot manage it. And if one places solid, heavy iron on the surface of the water, it sinks into it. Thus this subtle thing refuses to be overpowered by the water, while the strong and mighty are not spared from it. By this wisdom, God (glorified is He) keeps ships afloat on the surface of the water despite their weight and the weight of what they carry. Likewise, every hollow object into which air has entered does not sink, because air refuses to be submerged in water; so the laden, heavily loaded ship clings to it.

Reflect how this heavy, great body sought refuge in this subtle, light thing and clung to it until it was safe from drowning. This is like one who falls into a well and clings to the skirt of a strong, mighty man who prevents him from falling into the well, so he is saved by clinging to him. Glory be to Him who suspended this great, heavy vessel by this subtle air without any visible tie or knot. Among His signs is the cloud, subjugated between heaven and earth: how He (glorified is He) produces it by the winds, which stir it up like dust, then gathers it together and joins part of it to part, then the wind fertilizes it—and these are the ones He named "fertilizing" (lawaqih)—then drives it upon their backs to the land in need of it. When it overtakes the land and settles over it, it pours out its water upon it. He sends the wind upon it while it is in the air, and it scatters and disperses it so that it does not harm, nor demolish what falls upon it all at once. Then, when it has irrigated and taken what it needs, He withdraws from it and parts from it. Thus it is "the water-carriers of the earth," borne upon the backs of the winds.

In al-Tirmidhi and others, it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he saw a cloud, said: "This is the water-carrier of the earth, which God drives to a people who do not thank Him nor remember Him." The cloud is the bearer of the sustenance of the servants and others, by which their provision is carried. Al-Hasan, when he saw a cloud, would say: "By God, this is your provision, but you deprive yourselves of it through your sins and offences."

In the Sahih, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said:

"A man was in a barren land when he heard a voice in a cloud saying: 'Water the garden of so-and-so.' The cloud moved off until it reached a garden, and when it was in its midst, it poured out its water there. A man was there with a spade, directing the water with it. He said: 'What is your name, O servant of God?' He said: 'So-and-so,' using the name he had heard in the cloud."

In sum, when you reflect upon the thick, dark cloud, how you see it gather in a clear sky with no turbidity in it, and how God creates it whenever and however He wills, and how, despite its softness and looseness, it carries heavy water between heaven and earth until its Lord and Creator permits it to release what it carries of water, so it releases it and sends it down in drops, each drop in a specific measure determined by His wisdom and mercy. The cloud sprinkles the water upon the earth in sprinkles, and sends it down as separate drops that do not mix, one drop with another. Neither does the later one precede the earlier, nor the earlier delay the later; nor does a drop catch up with its companion to mix with it. Rather, each one descends along the path marked out for it, from which it does not deviate, until it strikes the earth drop by drop, each drop having been assigned to a part of the earth that it does not exceed to another. Even if all of creation gathered to create a single drop of it, or to count the number of raindrops in a single instant, they would be unable to do so.

Reflect how He (glorified is He) drives it as provision for the servants, the beasts, the birds, the ants and the locusts; He drives it as provision for such-and-such animal in such-and-such land beside such-and-such mountain, so that it reaches it in its state of great need and thirst at such-and-such a time. Then reflect how He deposited it in the earth, and then brought forth through it all kinds of foods, medicines and sustenance.

Know that after forty, a person begins to decline and his powers weaken gradually, just as he grew in strength gradually. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is He who created you in weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and grey hair.﴾

So his strength lies between two weaknesses, and his life between two deaths. He is first a *nutfah* (a drop of fluid), then an *alaqah* (a clinging clot), then a *mudghah* (a lump of flesh), then a *janin* (fetus) as long as he is in the womb. When he comes out, he is a *walid* (newborn). Until he completes seven days, he is a *sadigh*, with the letter *ghayn* marked with a dot, because his *sudgh* (temple) has not yet grown firm. As long as he nurses, he is a *radi'* (nursling). When milk is weaned from him, he is a *fatim* (weaned). When he crawls and begins to walk, he is a *darij*. The rajaz poet said:

"Would that I had visited, not as one going out, / but as a child who has crawled and then walked."

When his height reaches five spans, he is a *khumasi* (five-spanner). When his teeth fall out, he is *mathghur* (one whose teeth have fallen), and it is said he has been *thafir*. When new teeth grow after they fall, he is *muthghir*, a form with the root letters *th* and *th* together. When he reaches seven or near it, he is a *mumayyiz* (one who discerns). When he reaches ten, he is *mutara'ri'* and *nashi'* (growing up). When he approaches puberty, he is *yafi'* and *murahiq* and *munahiz lil-hulm* (near the age of maturity). When he reaches puberty, he is *baligh*. When his strength is gathered, he is a *hazwar*. His name in all of this is *ghulam* as long as his moustache has not appeared. When his moustache appears and the hair of his cheeks begins to rise, he is *baqil*, and his face has become *baqil*, with the form lightened. Then, from that point until his beard is complete, he is a *fata* and *shari'* (youth), because the prime of youth has come to him.

Al-Jawhari said: *al-fata* is the young man and *al-fatat* is the young woman. *Al-fata* is also used for a slave, even if he is a very old man. From this is the hadith: "Let none of you say 'my slave' or 'my female slave'; let him say 'my young man' and 'my young woman'." *Al-fata* is also said of the generous and noble man.

When his beard is complete, he is *shabb* (young man) until forty. Then he begins *kuhulah* (middle age) until sixty. Then he begins *shaykhukhah* (old age). When his hair begins to whiten, it is said he is *shab*. When it increases, it is said *washahu al-shayb* (grey has marked him). When it grows further, he is *shamat*. When his grey overcomes him, he is *aghtham*. When his head and beard are fully lit with grey, he is *mutaqa'is*. When his powers decline, he is *haram* (decrepit). When his conditions change and his deficiency appears, he has been returned to the lowest age, and death is closer to him than the hand is to the mouth.

(Subtlety)

Consider the names of the six who fought in the duel on the day of Badr, and how destiny arranged that their names matched their conditions on that day. The unbelievers were Shaybah, 'Utbah and al-Walid, three names of weakness. Al-Walid has the beginning of weakness, and Shaybah has the end of weakness, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God is He who created you in weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and grey hair.﴾

'Utbah is from *'utbah* (reproach), so their names indicated a reproach that would befall them and a weakness that would overtake them. Their counterparts among the Muslims were 'Ali, 'Ubaydah and al-Harith, may God be pleased with them, three names that correspond to their attributes: height (*'uluww*), servitude (*'ubudiyyah*), and striving, which is tilling (*harth*). They prevailed over them through their servitude and their striving in the tilling of the Hereafter.

(Exhortation)

The pleasure of a whole year is not worth an hour of grief, so how much more so when the matter is reversed?!

How many crocodiles lie in the sea of delusion. Beware, O diver: you will learn, O debtor, the story of yourself when the creditors take hold of you.

When every debtor meets his creditor, and there is delay [in payment],
you will learn, O Layla, what kind of debt you have incurred.

Whoever does not, with the tweezers of justice, pluck out the thorns of wrong from the hands of conduct, [leaves] a trace that cannot be safely assumed not to spread to the heart.

(Great Benefit)

The best thing that souls acquire and hearts attain, through which a servant gains elevation in this world and the Hereafter, is knowledge and faith. For this reason, He (Glorified is He) joined the two together in His saying: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have indeed remained, according to the Book of God, until the Day of Resurrection."﴾

And His saying: ﴿God will raise those among you who believe and those who were given knowledge by degrees.﴾

These are the essence of existence and its core, and the ones qualified for the lofty ranks. But most people are mistaken about the true reality of the names "knowledge" and "faith," through which happiness and nearness are attained, and about their reality, to the extent that every group thinks that what it possesses of knowledge and faith is the very thing by which happiness is attained. This is not so. Rather, most of them possess no faith that saves nor knowledge that elevates. Indeed, they have blocked off for their souls the paths of knowledge and faith that the Messenger brought and called the community to, and upon which he and his Companions after him stood, and those who followed them in their methodology and footsteps.

So every group believes that knowledge is what it possesses, and rejoices in it, and ﴿they have divided their affair among themselves into sects, each party rejoicing in what it has﴾.

Most of what they have is speech, opinions, and conjecture, and knowledge lies beyond speech, as Hammad ibn Zayd said:

I said to Ayyub: "Is knowledge today more abundant, or in what came before?"

He said: "Speech is more abundant today, and knowledge was more abundant in what came before."

This firmly rooted scholar distinguished between knowledge and speech. Books are very numerous, and speech, disputation, and mental speculations are numerous, but knowledge is far removed from most of them, and it is what the Messenger brought from God. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever argues with you about it after the knowledge has come to you﴾.

And He said: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge﴾, and He said about the Qur'an: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾, meaning: in it is His knowledge.

When the time since this knowledge grew long, the affair came to many people such that they took the fleeting thoughts of ideas, passing impulses, and opinions as knowledge, wrote books about them, spent their breaths on them, wasted time on them, filled pages with ink, and hearts with darkness, until many of them declared that there is no knowledge in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and that their proofs are merely verbal and yield neither certainty nor knowledge. Satan shouted this word among them and proclaimed it in their midst until its sound reached the near and far among them, and hearts were stripped of knowledge and faith by it, as a snake is stripped of its skin, and a garment from its wearer.

[Section on Tamakkun (Firm Establishment)]

The author of al-Manazil said:

(Chapter on Tamakkun) God Most High said: ﴿And let not those who have no certainty make you light (of heart)﴾ [al-Rum: 60].

The way in which this verse serves as evidence is most evident: the one who has attained tamakkun is not troubled by the abundance of distractions, nor by mixing with the people of heedlessness, nor by keeping company with the people of idleness. Rather, he has become firmly established through his patience and his certainty, so that they cannot provoke him or make him light. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of God is true﴾ [al-Rum: 60]. Whoever fulfils patience its due, and is certain that God's promise is true, will not be provoked by the falsifiers, nor will those who lack certainty make him light. Whenever his patience or his certainty weakens, or both, these people provoke him and those people make him light, and they draw him to themselves in proportion to the weakness of the strength of his patience and certainty. Thus, whenever that weakens in him, their pull upon him grows stronger, and whenever his patience and certainty grow stronger, his being drawn away from them and his pull upon them grow stronger.

(Section)

The Shaykh said: Tamakkun is above tuma'nina (serenity, tranquility), and it indicates the furthest point of stability.

Tamakkun is the capacity to exercise control over doing and refraining, and it is also called makana (standing, station). God Most High said: ﴿Say: O my people, act according to your standing; indeed I am acting [according to mine]﴾ [al-An'am: 135], and so on.

In the technical usage of this people, it is most often applied to one who has passed to the station of subsistence (baqa') after annihilation (fana'), which is what they call arrival (wusul). Its reality is the servant's triumph over his own self, which is that the rulings of human nature are concealed from him by the rising of the sun of Reality and the dominion of its authority. When this state endures for him, or prevails over him, he is one who possesses tamkin.

The author of al-Manazil said: Tamakkun is above tuma'nina, and it indicates the furthest point of stability. It is above tuma'nina because the latter exists alongside a kind of contention, so the heart becomes settled in what it dwells upon, though it may or may not become firmly established in it. For this reason tamakkun is the furthest point of stability. It is a form of tafa''ul (reflexive derivation) from makan (place), as if his station has become a place for his heart, which has taken it as an abode and a resting place.
